entries.title: Ability scores & modifiers
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma describe different physical and mental capabilities. Axria also uses Honor, governed by the campaign rules in its own section.

An ability score describes the capability; its modifier is the number usually added to a d20 roll. Calculate the modifier as (score − 10) ÷ 2, rounded down. For example, 9 gives −1, 14 gives +2, and 19 gives +4.

For the six standard abilities, 10–11 is the ordinary human baseline; 18 is exceptional. Adventurers normally have a maximum of 20 unless a feature says otherwise. Monsters and divine beings may reach 30. Honor is assigned by the DM rather than advanced normally.

Six abilities provide a quick description of every creature’s physical and mental characteristics:
Strength, measuring physical power
Dexterity, measuring agility
Constitution, measuring endurance
Intelligence, measuring reasoning and memory
Wisdom, measuring perception and insight
Charisma, measuring force of personality

entries.title: Score-to-modifier table
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use the modifier for checks and saving throws involving that ability. Apply proficiency and other bonuses only when the relevant rule allows them.

entries.title: Ability checks
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: The DM calls for an ability check when an attempted task has an uncertain outcome and a meaningful chance of failure. The DM chooses the ability and the Difficulty Class (DC).
Roll d20 + the chosen ability modifier + applicable bonuses. A total equal to or greater than the DC succeeds; a lower total fails, with the DM determining the consequences.

A skill is a particular application of an ability. A check may use an ability without any skill. Under the 2014 rules, a natural 1 or 20 does not automatically fail or succeed on an ordinary ability check.

entries.title: Typical Difficulty Classes
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: These are reference DCs. The DM sets the DC for the actual task; a specific rule may supply its own.

entries.title: Advantage & disadvantage
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: With advantage, roll two d20s and use the higher result. With disadvantage, use the lower. Neither stacks into additional dice.
If both advantage and disadvantage apply, they cancel: roll one d20, regardless of how many sources of either apply.
When a rule allows a reroll or replacement of a d20 while you have advantage or disadvantage, you can reroll or replace only one of the two dice, unless the rule says otherwise.

entries.title: Proficiency bonus
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Add your proficiency bonus when a skill, tool, attack, or saving throw proficiency applies. Your class level table gives the bonus; for a multiclass character it is based on total character level.
Apply the bonus only once to a roll. A feature such as Expertise can double it for specified uses; proficiency is not added a second time from another applicable source.
If a rule doubles or halves the bonus, do so only once for that roll. A multiplier cannot create a proficiency bonus for a check that would not normally receive one.

entries.title: Skills & other abilities
entries.label: 2014 rules · Includes variant
content: The usual skill–ability pairings appear under each ability. When the DM calls for Wisdom (Perception), for example, add Wisdom and add proficiency if you are proficient in Perception.

Variant: the DM may pair a skill with a different ability when the approach warrants it. A long swim could use Constitution (Athletics); a display of physical menace could use Strength (Intimidation). A relevant skill proficiency still applies.

entries.title: Contests
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: When two creatures directly oppose one another, both make the ability check appropriate to their own effort. Compare the totals rather than checking a fixed DC.
The higher total wins. On a tie, the situation remains as it was before the contest: a tied attempt to wrench away an object fails to change who holds it, for example.

entries.title: Passive checks
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: A passive check uses no die roll. The DM can use it for repeated efforts or to resolve something secretly.
Passive total = 10 + all modifiers that normally apply to the check. Add 5 for advantage, or subtract 5 for disadvantage. If both apply, they cancel.
Example: Wisdom 15 gives +2. With proficiency bonus +2 and Perception proficiency, passive Wisdom (Perception) is 14.

entries.title: Working together
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: One character makes the check with advantage when another character can meaningfully assist. In combat, providing this assistance requires the Help action.
The helper must be able to attempt the task alone, and cooperation must actually be useful. A task that requires a particular proficiency may prevent an untrained character from helping.

entries.title: Group checks
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: When the group succeeds or fails together, the DM may ask everyone to make an ability check.
If at least half the group succeeds, the group succeeds. Otherwise, it fails. This lets stronger participants compensate for weaker ones when cooperation is appropriate.

entries.title: Saving throws
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: A saving throw resists a threat such as a spell, trap, poison, or disease. The threatening effect normally tells you when to save, which ability to use, and the consequences.
Roll d20 + the relevant ability modifier. Add proficiency only if you are proficient in that saving throw, and include any other applicable modifiers.
Meet or exceed the effect’s save DC to succeed. Advantage, disadvantage, and situational bonuses can apply. Skills do not supply saving throw proficiency.

For a spell, the usual save DC is 8 + the caster’s spellcasting ability modifier + proficiency bonus. Specific effects may use another formula. Death saving throws have their own rules and do not use this ordinary ability-save formula.

entries.title: Strength — Overview
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Strength represents physical power, athletic capability, and the force you can exert.
Associated skill: Athletics.
Use Strength checks for brute force: moving heavy objects, breaking restraints, forcing an opening, or holding something in place.

entries.title: Athletics
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Strength (Athletics) for difficult climbing, jumping, or swimming.

items: Climb a slick or sheer surface, avoid hazards during a climb, or cling on while being dislodged.
Attempt an exceptional jump or a stunt during a leap.
Swim against dangerous currents, stay afloat in turbulent water, or resist being pulled underwater.

entries.title: Other Strength checks
entries.label: 2014 rules

items: Force a stuck, locked, or barred door.
Break bonds or force yourself through a tight passage.
Hold onto a moving wagon while dragged.
Topple a statue or stop a rolling boulder.

content: The DM decides whether a skill applies; raw Strength checks do not automatically use Athletics.

entries.title: Melee attacks & damage
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Strength is normally added to both the attack and damage rolls of a melee weapon.

Finesse weapons can use Strength or Dexterity, using the same ability for both rolls. A thrown melee weapon normally uses the same ability it would use in melee; a thrown finesse weapon can use either.

entries.title: Lifting & carrying
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: While pushing or dragging a load greater than your carrying capacity, your speed becomes 5 feet.
For each size category above Medium, double these limits. Tiny creatures halve them. Small creatures use the same limits as Medium creatures.

entries.title: Encumbrance — Variant
entries.label: 2014 rules · Optional variant
content: Use this optional system only if the DM adopts it. Ignore the Strength requirement column of the Armor table when using this variant.

rows: More than Strength × 10 lb, up to carrying capacity
Heavily encumbered: speed reduced by 20 ft; disadvantage on Strength, Dexterity, and Constitution ability checks, attack rolls, and saving throws

content: The heavily encumbered speed reduction is 20 feet total, not an additional 20 feet on top of the encumbered reduction.

entries.title: Dexterity — Overview
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Dexterity represents agility, balance, and quick reactions.
Associated skills: Acrobatics, Sleight of Hand, and Stealth.
It commonly affects ranged weapon attacks, finesse weapon attacks, Armor Class, and initiative.

entries.title: Acrobatics
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Dexterity (Acrobatics) to stay balanced or perform acrobatic movements.

items: Keep your footing on ice, a narrow rope, or a ship’s moving deck.
Perform a dive, roll, somersault, or flip when the outcome is uncertain.

content: It does not automatically replace Athletics for climbing, jumping distance, or other tasks based on force.

entries.title: Sleight of Hand
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) for discreet manual tricks.

items: Conceal an object on your person or secretly plant it on someone else.
Lift a coin purse or remove something from another person’s pocket.

entries.title: Stealth
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Dexterity (Stealth) to avoid notice: conceal yourself, slip past sentries, move away unseen, or approach without being heard.
The situation must permit hiding; a successful roll cannot make you hidden from a creature that clearly sees you. See Hiding & detection for the accompanying rules.

items: Control a loaded cart on a steep descent or steer a chariot through a tight turn.
Pick a lock or disable a trap when the required tools and proficiency allow it.
Tie a prisoner securely or wriggle out of bonds.
Play a stringed instrument or craft a small, intricate object.

entries.title: Attacks, Armor Class & initiative
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Dexterity is normally added to attack and damage rolls with ranged weapons. Finesse melee weapons can use Dexterity in place of Strength.

Armor determines how much Dexterity contributes to AC: light armor normally allows the full modifier, medium armor normally caps the bonus at +2, and heavy armor normally does not use it. Apply the actual armor or feature’s formula.
Initiative is a Dexterity check. A skill proficiency such as Acrobatics does not automatically apply.

entries.title: Hiding & detection
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: The DM decides whether the circumstances allow you to hide. Roll Dexterity (Stealth); until you are found or stop hiding, active searches use Wisdom (Perception) in a contest with your result.

A creature that sees you clearly prevents you from hiding from it. Noise can reveal your position. Being invisible permits an attempt to hide, but does not automatically make you hidden; sound or traces may still give you away.
A creature that is not actively searching may notice you through passive Wisdom (Perception). Compare its passive score against your Stealth result.
Approaching a creature in open view usually reveals you. Distraction or other circumstances may let you remain hidden at the DM’s discretion. Visibility and obscurement also matter.

entries.title: Constitution — Overview
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Constitution represents health, endurance, and bodily resilience.
No skills are normally associated with Constitution. A plain Constitution check can represent pushing your endurance beyond its ordinary limits.
Do not confuse Constitution checks with Constitution saving throws: the relevant task or effect decides which roll is used.

entries.title: Constitution checks
entries.label: 2014 rules

items: Hold your breath when the DM calls for an endurance check.
March or work for hours, or go without sleep.
Endure a shortage of food or water.
Drink a large quantity of ale in one attempt.

content: These are examples of situations involving endurance. Specific rules for suffocation, travel, starvation, or other hazards still determine when a check or saving throw is required.

entries.title: Hit points
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Your Constitution modifier normally contributes to the hit points you receive at each level and to Hit Dice rolls used to regain hit points.

If the modifier changes, adjust maximum hit points as though the new modifier had applied at every level. A +1 increase to the modifier at level 7 increases maximum hit points by 7; a −1 change reduces them by 7.
Use the specific class or effect’s instructions for the rest of the hit point calculation.

entries.title: Intelligence — Overview
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Intelligence represents reasoning, memory, education, and analysis.
Associated skills: Arcana, History, Investigation, Nature, and Religion.
Use it to recall knowledge, interpret clues, or solve a problem through deduction.

entries.title: Arcana
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Intelligence (Arcana) for this skill.
Recall knowledge about spells, magic items, magical symbols and traditions, planes of existence, and planar inhabitants.

entries.title: History
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Intelligence (History) for this skill.
Recall historical events, notable people, old kingdoms, earlier disputes and wars, or vanished civilizations.

entries.title: Investigation
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Intelligence (Investigation) for this skill.
Examine clues and draw conclusions: infer where something is hidden, identify a weapon from a wound, find a structural weak point, or search documents for the crucial evidence.

entries.title: Nature
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Intelligence (Nature) for this skill.
Recall knowledge about terrain, plants, animals, weather, and the workings of natural cycles.

entries.title: Religion
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Intelligence (Religion) for this skill.
Recall knowledge about deities, prayers, religious practices and organizations, sacred symbols, or cult traditions.

entries.title: Other Intelligence checks
entries.label: 2014 rules

items: Communicate an idea without speech.
Estimate the value of an object.
Assemble a convincing disguise or forge a document.
Recall how a craft or trade works.
Play a game whose outcome depends on skill.

content: A tool proficiency may be relevant when the DM calls for one; these examples are not automatic applications of Investigation.

entries.title: Spellcasting — Intelligence
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Wizards use Intelligence as their spellcasting ability. For their spells, it determines the ability modifier in spell attack rolls and saving throw DCs.
Spell attack bonus = Intelligence modifier + proficiency bonus. Spell save DC = 8 + Intelligence modifier + proficiency bonus. Follow a class or feature’s own text if it says otherwise.

entries.title: Wisdom — Overview
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Wisdom represents awareness, intuition, and sensitivity to what is happening around you.
Associated skills: Animal Handling, Insight, Medicine, Perception, and Survival.
Use it to read behaviour, notice danger, care for injuries, or navigate the natural world.

entries.title: Animal Handling
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Wisdom (Animal Handling) for this skill.
Calm a domesticated animal, keep a mount from panicking, judge an animal’s intentions, or control a mount during a risky maneuver.

entries.title: Insight
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Wisdom (Insight) for this skill.
Infer someone’s intentions from their body language, mannerisms, and behaviour. This can help you assess a possible lie or anticipate a move; it does not guarantee access to their thoughts.

entries.title: Medicine
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Wisdom (Medicine) for this skill.
Attempt to stabilize a dying creature or identify an illness. Other rules may supply the action and DC, such as the check to stabilize a creature.

entries.title: Perception
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Wisdom (Perception) for this skill.
Notice something through your senses: overhear a quiet conversation, detect movement nearby, or spot a hidden creature, object, or light.

entries.title: Survival
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Wisdom (Survival) for this skill.
Follow tracks, hunt, guide others through wilderness, recognize signs of nearby creatures, predict weather, or avoid natural hazards.

entries.title: Other Wisdom checks
entries.label: 2014 rules

items: Get an intuitive sense of which course of action to take.
Determine whether an apparently living or dead creature is actually undead.

content: The DM chooses whether these uses require a check and whether a particular skill applies.

entries.title: Spellcasting — Wisdom
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Clerics, druids, and rangers use Wisdom as their spellcasting ability.
Spell attack bonus = Wisdom modifier + proficiency bonus. Spell save DC = 8 + Wisdom modifier + proficiency bonus. A particular feature may specify another ability or formula.

entries.title: Charisma — Overview
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Charisma represents social presence, confidence, expression, and the ability to influence others.
Associated skills: Deception, Intimidation, Performance, and Persuasion.
It covers both forceful and subtle social approaches. A high Charisma score does not require kindness or honesty.

entries.title: Deception
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Charisma (Deception) for this skill.
Mislead someone with words or actions: tell a plausible lie, conceal the truth, pass off a disguise, make false assurances, cheat a mark, or hide your reaction.

entries.title: Intimidation
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Charisma (Intimidation) for this skill.
Influence someone through threats, hostility, or the prospect of violence: pressure a prisoner, deter attackers, or threaten a powerful official.

entries.title: Performance
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Charisma (Performance) for this skill.
Entertain an audience through music, dance, acting, storytelling, or another form of performance.

entries.title: Persuasion
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Use Charisma (Persuasion) for this skill.
Influence someone through tact, courtesy, or a good-faith appeal: obtain an audience, negotiate peace, make a cordial request, or inspire a community.

entries.title: Other Charisma checks
entries.label: 2014 rules

items: Find a useful person to ask about local news, gossip, or rumours.
Blend into a crowd to learn what people are talking about.

content: The approach and the circumstances determine whether a skill applies. A social check does not guarantee that another creature will agree to an impossible demand.

entries.title: Spellcasting — Charisma
entries.label: 2014 rules
content: Bards, paladins, sorcerers, and warlocks use Charisma as their spellcasting ability.
Spell attack bonus = Charisma modifier + proficiency bonus. Spell save DC = 8 + Charisma modifier + proficiency bonus. Follow the relevant class or feature if it gives different instructions.

entries.title: Honor — Overview
entries.label: Axria homebrew
content: Honor measures virtue, trustworthiness, and integrity. It reflects how well a character behaves and how considerate they remain, especially when circumstances are difficult.
Honor does not determine whether a character is a “good person.” It reflects their conduct, principles, and consideration for others rather than assigning moral alignment.
Honor has no associated skills. It is rarely called upon, but when it matters, it can have greater significance than the other ability scores.

entries.title: Earning & losing Honor
entries.label: Axria homebrew
content: Honor is earned or lost through a character’s behaviour. The DM is responsible for deciding its value based on how the character acts.
Ability Score Improvements and other features that normally alter ability scores do not change Honor. Changes come from the DM’s judgement of the character’s conduct.
This rule does not assign a fixed starting score, a reward table, or automatic increases and penalties. Those decisions remain with the DM.

entries.title: Honor checks
entries.label: Axria homebrew
content: The DM may call for an Honor check to determine how justly, diplomatically, or honorably a character behaves in an important situation.

These checks are particularly relevant when dealing with officials such as guards, nobles, and other authorities. They can test whether a character upholds standards of conduct when the situation puts those standards under pressure.
Honor has no associated skill proficiency. The DM sets the stakes and decides when the check is appropriate.

entries.title: Honor saving throws
entries.label: Axria homebrew
content: The DM may call for an Honor saving throw when a character’s will and determination are tested by an outside source attempting to break or humiliate them.
The save concerns maintaining dignity, resolve, and integrity under that pressure. It is a rare roll with potentially significant consequences.
The DM decides when it applies and what success or failure means. This homebrew does not automatically replace the saving throw named by a spell or other existing effect.

entries.title: Honor at the table
entries.label: Axria homebrew
content: Use Honor sparingly, when the character’s conduct or determination carries particular weight. The value follows behaviour; it cannot be improved by ordinary character-building choices.
Honor checks concern acting justly, diplomatically, or honorably. Honor saving throws concern withstanding an external attempt to break or humiliate the character.
The distinction from Charisma is the focus: Charisma concerns social influence and expression; Honor concerns integrity and conduct. Which ability applies depends on what is actually being tested.
